transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-04
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Chen (LatticeMed), Leo Martinez (Platform), Sasha Kim (CISO)
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/security (security pack), doc: /drive/LatticeMed/samples (sample payloads), spreadsheet: /sheets/latticemed-benchmarks

Summary: quick walkthrough of Console's trace mapping, request-forensics flow, and how KV cache fallback looks in traces. Discussed security requirements, replay plan, and next steps for pilot.

Topics covered: trace correlation IDs, prefix / KV cache hits vs misses, routing fallbacks, model variant rollbacks, request replay, audit logging, encrypted logs, canary testing.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, we've got about 45 minutes, we'll focus on the console trace mapping and a little forensics example. Maya will drive the demo.
[00:18] Dr. Chen: Great, we just want to see how you map a user request through the different runtime stages and how we can spot when the kv cache falls back that was causing extra latency for us.
[00:30] Maya: Perfect, so I'll share my screen — starting on the Console Requests page. Note: transcription may flip "KV cache" sometimes to "K V cache" in the recording.
[00:45] Maya: Here's a single request in the last 24 hours, you'll see the trace id at the top, request fingerprint, and a breakdown of spans. The trace correlates HTTP ingress, routing, batch enqueue, model host execution, and response assembly.
[01:15] Leo: Can you show the raw logs side-by-side? We want to match our platform logs to the Console trace.
[01:25] Maya: Yup. There's a linked request-log tab. We include timestamped events and the raw wire payload. See here — you can filter on request-id or session id.
[01:40] Maya: Notice an early span shows "prefetch: prefix-key check" — that's Redwood's prefix caching layer. If there's a miss, the next span shows "kv_cache_fallback" and then the full model call.
[02:05] Dr. Chen: In our tests we saw intermittent 400s that looked like tokenization errors, but maybe it was a fallback triggering a model variant that didn't do the same preprocessing?
[02:20] Maya: Exactly a good hypothesis. We often see two error modes — preprocessing mismatch or truncated KV cache entries that make the model get a shorter context and error. You can expand the span to see the preprocessor stdout, sometimes transcribed as "pre-proc" in logs.
[03:00] Alex: Quick note — we redact PII in the console view but we keep a full encrypted trace bundle that you can request for deeper internal debugging. Sasha, I know you wanted to confirm encryption & retention?
[03:18] Sasha: Yes, we need to ensure the traces are encrypted at rest and that RBAC controls only allow audit access. Also, do you store full raw request bodies by default?
[03:30] Alex: By default we keep redacted payloads in the UI. Full raw bundles are stored encrypted and require a KMS key binding + explicit request for export. We'll put the network diagram and KMS flow in the security pack.
[03:55] Maya: Back to the trace, I'm going to demonstrate a request replay. We have a built-in replay tool — press replay and it will send the exact payload back through the chosen routing policy and model variant.
[04:20] Maya: I'm selecting the "simulate KV miss" checkbox to force the fallback path so you can see the latencies diverge. Starting replay now.
[04:40] [04:40] Maya: Replay run #1 shows 180ms tail latency with KV hit, Replay run #2 forced miss shows 820ms and a model fallback to a quantized variant we use for low-cost routing.
[05:10] Leo: That's the behavior we suspected. When we saw higher latencies, did you also see token-level spikes?
[05:22] Maya: Yes, expand the model host span and you'll get per-token timing. The UI shows token throughput and where batching caused head-of-line waits. Sometimes the transcript parser shows that as "token per sec" or "tps"; labels vary.
[05:50] Dr. Chen: When a fallback to a quantized model happens, do you get automatic quality regression alerts? We run prompt sets nightly.
[06:05] Maya: Good question. Redwood Optimize hooks into our evals; if the quantized variant's outputs deviate past your configured thresholds, we send a regression alert and can auto-fallback the route until manual review. We can link those alerts to traces for the failing requests.
[06:35] Alex: Also, you can pin a customer to Dedicated capacity to avoid the routing-to-quantized behavior at the cost of reserved GPUs. That's in the quote.
[06:50] Leo: For our compliance, we need immutable audit logs showing who viewed a trace and when. Is that available?
[07:00] Maya: Yes, audit trail shows view events, exports, and replay launches. Each entry includes actor, timestamp, and the CRN. We can export the audit CSV for your SIEM.
[07:18] [07:18] Maya: I'm scrolling to an actual error example. Here the span shows an "encoder failed" error — the raw log shows "utf-8 decode err" but the UI sometimes munges it to "utf decode error" due to ASR.
[07:45] Dr. Chen: That looks like it came from a non-UTF payload in user messages — we have an edge case where devices send malformed bytes. How would you suggest we handle this?
[07:58] Maya: We recommend pre-normalizing in your ingress with a lightweight preprocessor. Meanwhile, console provides a per-route nuance: you can add a preprocessor hook so those requests are normalized before hitting the model.
[08:20] Maya: Now I'm switching to trace mapping — you can group requests by fingerprint patterns. For example, requests that hit the same prefix key will cluster; that helps find common cache thrashers.
[08:45] [08:45] Alex: One feature many customers like: request heatmaps over time. You can see spikes in misses correlated with deployments or upstream changes.
[09:05] Leo: Can we ingest our own logs and join them to the trace in your UI? We have internal correlation IDs.
[09:18] Maya: Yes, we support ingestion via a small sidecar or forwarder; you can map your correlation id to Redwood's request-id at ingest time. We can show a combined timeline.
[09:40] Dr. Chen: Could you demo a canary rollback? We had a bad rollout last month and it'd help to see the fallback decisions.
[09:55] Maya: Sure, in the rollout tab you can see traffic split, percentage, and automatic fallback triggers. If a variant exceeds error thresholds for more than X minutes, it flips traffic back to the previous variant. In the trace view you'll see a rollout-span noting the switch.
[10:30] Maya: I'm going to open a trace where a canary triggered a rollback — notice the orange span "rollout-eval" and then the subsequent "route-change" event. We also capture the metrics snapshot used to make that decision.
[11:05] Alex: These metrics are what we use to power auto-fallbacks and alerts. You can tune the sensitivity per route.
[11:20] [11:20] Leo: About request replays — when you replay, does it hit production or an isolated instance? We need reproducibility without affecting customer quotas.
[11:35] Maya: Replays can be run in "shadow" or "replay" mode. Shadow sends to a mirror stack (no impact), while replay can hit a test variant. We recommend shadow for initial debugging.
[11:50] Dr. Chen: For the shadow replays, how do you handle stateful operations? Some of our backends are not idempotent.
[12:05] Maya: The replay tool rewrites connectors to use mock backends or a replay sandbox you provide. If you have non-idempotent endpoints, you can supply a replay translation mapping to safely stub calls.
[12:30] [12:30] Maya: I'm going to show a forensic example now: we take a failing request, expand spans, look at env variables captured at the host (like model version, quantization, batch id), and then we fetch the exact prompt tokens so you can run a local reproduce.
[12:55] Dr. Chen: Can we get the tokenized prompt export? We want to run the same tokenization in-house.
[13:08] Maya: Yes, token stream is exportable in the trace bundle. It includes tokenizer version and exact bytes.
[13:25] Leo: Are these bundles stored outside our tenant? We need guarantees about access and deletion.
[13:35] Alex: Bundles are tenant-scoped, encrypted with your KMS. You can set retention policy and revoke access at any time; we'll put the retention setting in the contract.
[13:55] Sasha: Also, log retention duration — our policy is 90 days for full logs, 1 year for redacted. Is that supported?
[14:10] Alex: We can configure retention tiers per customer; 90 days full + 1 year redacted is a common pattern.
[14:25] [14:25] Maya: Next, watch this KV cache thrash example — filter traces by fingerprint frequency and sort by miss-rate. See the cluster where a misbehaving client kept writing slightly different prefixes, breaking cache hits.
[14:55] Dr. Chen: That's interesting — the device-side ID had a timestamp suffix. We can normalize that at the edge but it would be useful for Console to show smart-grouping heuristics.
[15:10] Maya: We do fuzzy fingerprint grouping; it's off by default but we can enable heuristics to group similar prefixes. I'll note that as an ask.
[15:32] Alex: Action: we should run a short experiment enabling fuzzy grouping for LatticeMed to confirm the cluster merges.
[15:45] [15:45] Maya: Moving on — error analysis page: you can create a saved query for errors over the last 7 days and attach a signal set of example requests. That becomes a regression test in Redwood Optimize.
[16:05] Dr. Chen: So we could tie our nightly evals to that saved query and get notified?
[16:12] Maya: Yup. We can trigger an alert when the sample prompts fail quality thresholds or when error-rate crosses a percent.
[16:35] Maya: I'm going to simulate a 5% error spike using the bench runner. Watch the error spike and the alert firing in the top-right.
[16:50] [16:50] Alex: And at this point you can drill into the impacted requests and either hotfix at the preprocessor or pin to a previous model variant while you investigate.
[17:05] Leo: Regarding per-token costs, can we annotate traces with cost breakdown? We saw a bill anomaly last month and need token-level cost visibility.
[17:18] Maya: The console shows token counts, effective compute units, and an estimated cost. It can also map to billed units if you want to reconcile.
[17:40] Dr. Chen: For the pilot, we need a runbook: steps to collect a failing request, export trace bundle, run replay in sandbox, and escalate to Redwood SE. Can you provide that?
[17:55] Alex: Yes, we'll send the runbook and sample playbook — that's part of the onboarding kit.
[18:10] [18:10] Maya: Time permitting, I'll show one more — a cross-tenant routing failure where traffic accidentally routed to a legacy model. In the trace you see a routing rule mismatch because the route tag didn't match the header key.
[18:30] Leo: We had a similar bug — header casing differences. Does Redwood normalize headers?
[18:38] Maya: We normalize common headers but custom headers need mapping. The route-matcher supports case-insensitive matching, but it depends on the rule config.
[18:55] Dr. Chen: Can Redwood webhooks give us immediate notifications of routing rule changes? We want to catch accidental edits.
[19:05] Alex: Yes, audit and webhook integration are available; we can post to your ops channel on changes.
[19:20] [19:20] Maya: Quick demo of the trace timeline export — clicking export bundles the trace and includes an action log. I'll export and show the download link (redacted in recording).
[19:45] Maya: Sending now — you should see an email link.
[19:55] Leo: Got it.
[20:05] [20:05] Dr. Chen: A quick security Q: When you do replays, are keys and secrets masked? We must ensure no downstream secrets leak to the Redwood sandbox.
[20:20] Maya: Replay tooling can scrub connector secrets and replace them with placeholders. We also support injecting mocked credentials so nothing sensitive leaves your environment.
[20:40] Alex: On the commercial side, I'll follow up with Dedicated vs Hosted TCO. If you want strict data residency + no egress, Private deployment is an option.
[20:55] Dr. Chen: Good. We prefer Private if the overhead isn't huge.
[21:05] Maya: For Private, Console behavior is the same; only the control plane and data plane choices differ.
[21:20] [21:20] Maya: I'm going to walk through a final failure cascade: tokenization error -> preproc fix -> replay -> verify.
[21:40] Maya: Step 1: capture request id. Step 2: export bundle. Step 3: run shadow replay with preproc normalization. Step 4: confirm metrics. Running now.
[22:05] [22:05] Replay complete — normalized payload passes; error gone.
[22:20] Dr. Chen: That's the flow we wanted. If you send the runbook we'll try it end-to-end.
[22:35] Alex: I'll also include a short troubleshooting checklist for SREs.
[22:45] [22:45] Leo: One integration ask: can the Console push a Slack thread to our #ml-ops with links to the trace and a short summary?
[22:55] Maya: Yes, we have a Slack integration; it posts a compact card with request id, error summary, and a link gated by SSO.
[23:10] Sasha: From a compliance side we need SSO + SAML enforced. Also IP allowlists for UI access.
[23:25] Alex: Both supported. We'll attach SSO setup docs. IP allowlists are configurable on Private and Dedicated; in hosted we support org-level allowlist.
[23:45] [23:45] Maya: Wrapping up — I'll note two engineering follow-ups: fuzzy-grouping heuristics and a sample script to auto-export tokenized prompt.
[24:00] Dr. Chen: Thanks, that was super helpful.
[24:10] Alex: Recap of next steps: send security pack, run replay with your sample requests, share quote and pilot timeline.
[24:25] Maya: Any final Qs?
[24:30] Dr. Chen: None from me. We'll coordinate offline about the pilot window.
[24:35] Leo: We'll upload the sample logs and IDs by Friday.
[24:40] Sasha: Expect follow-up questions on retention and audit exports.
[24:45] Alex: Great, thanks everyone.

End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional misattribution (Speaker 1/2), ASR sometimes alters technical tokens (KV -> K V), and punctuation is inconsistent.
